blocks.content: The Competition Act, 2002 shifted the regulatory paradigm from curbing monopolies under the MRTP Act to promoting free and fair market competition.

rows: Curbing concentration of economic power and monopolies
Promoting market competition and protecting consumer interest
Firm size and asset threshold (Structural approach)
Market conduct and anti-competitive behavior (Behavioral approach)
Only the 'abuse' of dominance is illegal, not dominance per se
Mandatory registration of restrictive trade agreements required
No registration needed; anti-competitive agreements are void per se
Limited powers; primarily issued cease-and-desist orders
Heavy financial penalties up to 10% of average turnover

items: Raghavan Committee (1999) is frequently asked as the advisory panel that recommended replacing the MRTP Act with a modern competition law framework.
MRTP Act targeted firm size and asset thresholds, whereas the Competition Act strictly targets the abuse of dominant position rather than dominance itself.
Appeals against orders passed by the CCI were originally heard by COMPAT, but are now heard by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act, 1969 was repealed and replaced by the Competition Act, 2002 based on the recommendations of the S.V.S. Raghavan Committee.
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) was established in 2003 as a quasi-judicial regulatory body to ensure fair competition in Indian markets.
While the MRTP Act focused on curbing monopolies based on asset size, the Competition Act focuses on market behavior and anti-competitive practices.
The Competition Act covers three main pillars: prohibition of anti-competitive agreements, prohibition of abuse of dominant position, and regulation of combinations (mergers and acquisitions).
